transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-02-11 16:00 PST | Duration: 46 minutes | Attendees: Maya C (Redwood AE), Diego A (Redwood SE), Ellen P (CTO, Zenith), Marco L (Lead ML Eng), Sophie N (Product), Aaron B (Infra)

Summary:
- Intro to Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private options for a rapid prototype and production path. Discussed PLG/onramp (free credits), security needs (SSO, KMS, audit logs), and time-to-first-token expectations. Agreed to a short benchmark and sandbox with credits.

Topics:
- Quickstart and free credits
- Hosted API vs Dedicated capacity vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Security/compliance: SOC 2, SSO, KMS, data retention
- Perf expectations: P50/P95 latency, throughput, batching
- Pilot scope and timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chopra: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call, then I'll hand over to Marco for the technical goals. uh we've got about 45 minutes, cool?
[00:10] Ellen Park: Yep thanks Maya. Ellen here, CTO at Zenith.
[00:12] Marco Li: Marco, lead ML engineer.
[00:14] Sophie Nguyen: Sophie, product.
[00:15] Aaron Bell: Aaron infra.
[00:18] Diego Alvarez: Diego here, Redwood SE.

[00:22] Maya Chopra: Awesome. Goal for today — understand what you need to go from prototype to pilot, what constraints you have, and whether hosted, dedicated, or private makes sense. also talk credits and time-to-first-token. Marco, do you want to kick off with current architecture?

[00:35] Marco Li: Sure. So right now we run a microservices stack on EKS. Our inference is a simple transformer-based reranker and a customer-facing chat feature. For prototype we used hosted APIs from a few vendors, but we hit variability in latency and cost. We're looking at a path that starts hosted for speed then maybe moves to dedicated or private for predictable costs and compliance. Key constraints: P95 latency < 250ms for reranking at batch sizes of ~8, and per-token cost needs to be under $0.0009 ideally. We also require audit logs and KMS for any customer data retention.

[01:12] Diego Alvarez: Got it, those are very typical. When you say hosted today, is that through public SaaS endpoints or self-hosted in your cloud?

[01:18] Marco Li: Public SaaS, some OpenAI, some open models via managed endpoints. Latency spikes during peak periods and token cost spiked last month—unexpected added 40% to our invoice.

[01:28] Maya Chopra: Right. Our PLG credits are meant to help here: we can provision a sandbox project, attach 50k tokens in credits so you can run realistic workloads and see the latency profile. That keeps your finance folks happy while you do the bench. Diego — can you run through the hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs briefly?

[01:44] Diego Alvarez: Sure. Hosted is fastest to get started: single API, streaming, webhooks — time-to-first-token typically under an hour for basic calls if you use our SDK. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity, so predictable throughput and lower unit costs at scale; it's a month-to-month reserved pool with burst options. Private (VPC or on-prem) is for when you need full network control, KMS integration/HSM, and auditability — takes more setup (weeks) and we offer an enterprise installer and private control plane.

[02:12] Sophie Nguyen: For our PM perspective, what does the developer experience look like for a quickstart? We need the product team to spin up a sandbox without infra help.

[02:21] Maya Chopra: Good question. PLG flow: self-serve sign-up, SDKs in Node/Python, quickstart templates for chat/rerank, and a console to view per-route costs. We'll create a sandbox project and share a starter repo. Time-to-first-token for a dev: minutes to get the first call, an hour for integration tests. For a realistic end-to-end prototype including data and perf benches expect the 1–2 day range with our credits.

[02:46] Aaron Bell: When you say KMS integration in private, can you clarify? We use GCP KMS and want customer-managed keys, not Redwood-managed.

[02:53] Diego Alvarez: Yes, private deployments support customer KMS/HSM integration. For hosted we offer envelope encryption at rest; enterprise customers can provision a key in their GC KMS and we can integrate for Dedicated or Private control plane — we exchange a few config artifacts and rotate keys per policy. That said, hosted with KMS-backed envelope encryption is slightly different from a private control plane where the keys never leave your VPC.

[03:17] Marco Li: How about audit logs? We need per-token level traceability for compliance.

[03:22] Diego Alvarez: We capture request/response metadata (not raw sensitive customer content unless requested). For Dedicated and Private you get extended retention and per-route tracing. We also support SAML SSO and RBAC for the console. We can provide SOC 2 and ISO docs — Maya will share them.

[03:37] Ellen Park: Good. Another question: we use short context lengths but sometimes long retrieval chains for customer support. Does Redwood handle dynamic batching and KV cache to lower token counts?

[03:48] Diego Alvarez: Yep — runtime does prefix/KV caching and continuous batching when it makes sense. You can configure caching policies per model/route. That often cuts token spend and latency for repeated contexts.

[04:00] Sophie Nguyen: In terms of cost predictions — do you have a cost estimation tool or numbers for the models you host? We need to model worst-case spend for our finance team.

[04:09] Maya Chopra: We provide per-model cost profiles in the model catalog and the console has token-level cost visibility. For the sandbox we'll share expected unit costs and a spreadsheet showing tradeoffs for hosted vs ded — that should help the finance model. We'll also recommend quantization or a smaller model for reranking if that meets quality.

[04:28] Marco Li: Can you run benchmarks against our sample prompt set? We need to see P50/P95 and tokens/sec on dedicated versus hosted.

[04:35] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. For the pilot we'll run a controlled bench using your prompt set. Ideally we get a representative dataset and your concurrency targets. Marco, can you send that? We'll run hosted first with your sandbox credits then spin up a small dedicated pool to compare.

[04:49] Marco Li: Yes I can. I will send a csv of 500 prompts and expected concurrency by EOD tomorrow.

[04:55] Maya Chopra: Perfect. On timeline — if we provision sandbox credits today, you could begin tests within 24 hours. If you decide to move to a dedicated pool, that setup is usually 3–5 business days once the contract is signed. Private deployments are longer — often 2–4 weeks depending on network and KMS handshake.

[05:11] Aaron Bell: For dedicated, do we need to ship any infra-side pieces? Like peering or endpoints in our VPC?

[05:18] Diego Alvarez: For dedicated, we offer two options: routed public endpoints with IP allow lists, or VPC peering/PrivateLink to your account. The private network option is common for enterprise infra teams; we can do a short network design session if you go that route.

[05:32] Sophie Nguyen: Any gotchas for plg onboarding? E.g. rate limiting or quotas that might block our prototype tests?

[05:38] Maya Chopra: We'll set quotas per project to protect both sides. For the sandbox we set elevated quotas but still finite — we'll work with you to ensure it's enough to run the bench. Also, SDKs support streaming and fine-grained retries to handle transient throttles.

[05:51] Marco Li: On the security paperwork: can you provide SOC 2 reports, and do you have a standard data processing agreement? Our legal will need those before any dedicated or private engagement.

[06:00] Maya Chopra: Yes, we'll share SOC 2, our DPA template, and the private deployment checklist. I'll drop them in the shared folder and include a short note on expected timelines for signature.

[06:10] Ellen Park: Sounds good. One more: competitors — we evaluated Anthropic and OpenAI; Anthropic had better alignment safety but cost was higher. Any Redwood-specific differentiators we should call out during negotiation?

[06:22] Diego Alvarez: Our main differentiator is the production-first runtime and the unified control plane across hosted/dedicated/private. That plus built-in caching/batching and model switching policies tends to reduce unit economics while keeping latency SLOs. For teams like yours who may start hosted and decide to reserve capacity, the same API and rollout controls make the migration lower risk.

[06:45] Sophie Nguyen: Okay that's helpful.

[06:48] Maya Chopra: Next steps recap: we'll provision a sandbox project with 50k credits and a starter repo; Diego will coordinate the bench and run hosted vs dedicated comparisons; I'll send SOC2, DPA, pricing, and pilot agreement; Marco will send sample prompts and concurrency targets. Schedule — can we target the bench next Thursday 2/18 for a deeper perf session?

[07:10] Marco Li: That works.

[07:12] Ellen Park: Works for us.

[07:15] Maya Chopra: Great. Anything else? 

[07:18] Aaron Bell: One small thing — monitoring hooks: do you expose OpenTelemetry traces or a webhook for error events?

[07:24] Diego Alvarez: We support tracing integration and can emit traces to your monitoring stack via OTLP or push alerts to webhooks. We'll include configuration examples in the repo.

[07:33] Sophie Nguyen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email after the bench.

[07:37] Maya Chopra: Thanks all — I'll send the items and booking invite for 2/18. Bye!

[end]

Notes on transcription: occasional transcription errors were corrected where obvious but some names might be slightly off in the automated export. Timestamp markers approximate conversation turns. Some filler 'uh'/'yeah' present in original audio.
